scenario.note: A production cap applied across the entire horizon restricts the total food output per month, forcing a reevaluation of blending and purchasing decisions.
The hardness of oil OIL2 is changed directly in the oils table. The original value is 4.2, so this is a reconfirmation of the base case. If a different value is intended, it should be specified.
A 10% reduction in hardness for every raw oil is modeled as a scale factor of 0.9 on the hardness parameter for each oil.
A minimum storage requirement is specified per month and oil, but here it is applied to the total storage in February across all oils.
The hardness of VEG1 is changed directly in the oils table. The original value is 8.8, so a change would require a new value specified here.
A cap on total oil bought per oil type is added as a rule over the buy decision measure across all oils.
The hardness of VEG2 is increased by 20%. This affects the blend hardness constraint and may alter purchase, storage, and refining decisions to maintain the hardness within bounds.
A uniform price change across all months and oils is modeled as a scale factor applied to the purchase price across all (month, oil) pairs.
The opening stock per oil is changed to a different value; the scenario tests sensitivity to initial inventory levels.
The oil hardness values are uniformly scaled down by 50% and the product hardness bounds are tightened to 4–5.5.
An upper limit on tons of oil refined is modeled as a rule on the consume measure per category and month, restricting the total refined oil per month per line.
The minimum tons of oil refined refers to the total consumption of a specific oil type (VEG1) over the horizon, with a target of at least 820 tons.

The oil hardness changes across the board; a uniform scaling is applied to hardness values. The resulting blend hardness constraints are adjusted to reflect the new values, with a relative rule ensuring the product hardness remains within bounds.
The hardness of VEG2 is changed from 6.1 to 6.5 in the raw oils table.
